To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) and dioxin-like compounds, including polychlorinated dioxins and dibenzofuranes, decrease levels of I-compounds in liver, the major organ for I-compound synthesis and accumulation in the body, in a structure-dependent, Ah receptor-dependent manner.

1) I-compounds are reduced in rat liver by various tumor promoters/cancerogens and that 2) the reduction is structure-dependent, i.e., it is more pronounced for Ah receptor agonists than for non-agonists.

the effects of the PCDFs on hepatic I-compounds were structure-dependent and paralleled those of Ah receptor agonists on Ah receptor binding and aryl hydrocarbon (Ah) hydroxylase induction, and that the effects on hepatic I compounds were consistent with the hypothesis that Ah receptor-mediated induction of cytochrome (CYP) P450 enzymes contributes to the decreased levels of I-compounds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of biomarkers that are useful for the early detection of tumor promotion/carcino-genesis, and our studies have demonstrated that I-compounds may fulfill such a role.
the elucidation of the mechanism(s) of tumor promotion/carcino-genesis.
the identification of chemical and biochemical mechanisms that are involved in the initiation and promotion stages of carcinogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PCDFs, like TCDD, affect hepatic I- compounds in a structure-dependent fashion, and the observed effects are consistent with an Ah receptor-mediated mechanism.
Ah receptor-mediated induction of cytochrome(s) P450 plays an important role in the effects of the PCDFs on I-compound formation, and that such effects may contribute to tumor promoting activity.
the present results support the notion that hepatic I-compounds represent useful biomarkers to monitor the biological effects of TCDD and related compounds.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the I-compound pattern and levels in rat hepatic DNA are sensitive to a variety of chemicals, including tumor promoters/carcino-gens, and the effects are structure-dependent, thus providing an opportunity to use the I-compound patterns as a mechanistic probe of chemical carcinogenesis.

I-compounds may be useful biomarkers for the detection of exposure to Ah receptor agonist chemicals and that their levels may also reflect the extent of Ah receptor-mediated enzyme-induction and/or tumor-promoting activity.

the Ah receptor plays an important role in tumor promotion/carcino- genesis by affecting I-compound patterns in liver DNA, and that this effect is mediated by Ah receptor-mediated enzyme inductions, especially of cytochrome p450.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the I-compound levels and patterns in hepatic DNA can be affected by a variety of chemical carcinogens.
the effects of the toxins are structure dependent.
the effects on DNA I-compounds are similar to the effects of these chemicals on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor.
